title: Are You Giving Out Lots Of Warnings? Here’s How To Fix It ow-to-fix-it/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Responding to one of SCM's most-requested topics, Michael Linsin addresses teacher concern over giving out too many first-level warnings. He reassures readers that a high volume of warnings, so long as most students don't escalate to further consequences, can actually indicate the plan is working as intended. He rejects the common fear that students are 'gaming' warnings as a free pass, arguing instead that frequent warnings for a particular rule usually mean the purpose of that rule hasn't been emotionally internalized by students. His recommended fix is to identify which rule triggers the most warnings and reteach it in a way that builds genuine empathy—helping students understand, viscerally, how their behavior affects classmates—rather than simply repeating the rule's wording. Once students grasp the rule's purpose empathetically, Linsin argues, warnings for that rule will decrease.
points: A high volume of first-level warnings can actually be a sign the classroom management plan is working, provided most students don't escalate to further consequences.
Linsin dismisses the common fear that students exploit warnings as a 'freebie'—he argues this rarely occurs, especially among elementary-age students.
Frequent warnings for a particular rule typically indicate students haven't emotionally internalized why that rule matters, not that they're gaming the system.
The recommended fix is to identify the rule triggering the most warnings and reteach it in a way that builds empathetic understanding of its purpose.
Helping students see the rule through the eyes of affected classmates—rather than simply restating it—is the key to reducing repeated warnings over time.
